summary: Gives an overview of DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), which lets an organization take responsibility for a message by signing it. It shows how DKIM fits into email services and how it relates to other message-signature technologies, for adopters, developers and deployers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: DKIM is like a wax seal on a letter that proves which organization sent it. This is a friendly guide to what the seal is for and how it fits with other ways of stamping mail.

questions: what does a dkim signature not do
subtitle: A guided tour of DKIM: how a domain can sign an email so receivers can verify who took responsibility for it.

tldr.problem: The origin of an email is often falsely stated, and judging mail by the sending IP address has known weaknesses and does not match organizational boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: DKIM lets a domain owner sign selected headers and the body with a private key, put the result in a DKIM-Signature header field, and publish the matching public key in the DNS for any verifier to fetch.
tldr.outcome: A valid signature ties a message to a verifiable domain (the SDID) and shows the message was not changed since signing, but it does not by itself say whether the message is good. That judgment is left to other services.

today: RFC 5585 is an Informational document from July 2009 and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an overview, not a standard; the protocol itself is specified in RFC 4871.

sections.title: What This Overview Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5585 describes the architecture and functionality of DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), the core mechanism for signing and verifying email messages. It is written for people adopting, developing or deploying DKIM, and for those thinking about extending it. It does not cover threats (see RFC 4686) or protocol details (see RFC 4871).

The core idea is that an organization can take responsibility for a message in a way a recipient can verify. That organization can be the author's, the originating site, an intermediary, or an independent service helping one of them. The document is explicit that DKIM is one basic tool in what needs to be a large arsenal against spam, phishing and similar abuse, and is not sufficient on its own.
sections.eli5: DKIM lets a company sign its emails so others can check who really sent them. It is one helpful tool, not a magic shield against bad mail.

sections.title: Scope and the Value Proposition
sections.content:
DKIM uses a domain name as the identifier of the responsible party. It is called the Signing Domain IDentifier (SDID) and sits in the d= tag of the DKIM-Signature header field. Whoever signs chooses the SDID, so the reputation of that domain can be used to decide whether to trust the message.

DKIM does the first of two jobs: it determines a verified identity that takes responsibility for the message. Evaluating how trustworthy that identity is remains a separate step. A valid signature neither raises nor lowers trust by itself. It also tells the receiver the signed content was not modified between signing and verifying.

The RFC lists what a signature alone does not do. It does not certify the contents such as the author From field beyond data integrity, make assertions about the signer's behavior, prescribe receiver actions, protect after verification, or protect against replay of an already signed message.

Replay is a real gap: a recipient or intermediary can re-post a signed message as a new message and the original signature still verifies.
sections.eli5: The seal says who stamped the letter and that it was not changed. It does not say the sender is nice, and anyone could photocopy a sealed letter and send it again.

sections.title: Design Goals and How DKIM Differs
sections.content:
DKIM adds end-to-end authentication on top of existing email relaying, so only the signer and the verifier need to support it. Its functional goals include domain-level granularity (an organization or department rather than an individual), signing by any party along the path, delegation of signing to independent parties, separating core authentication from the policies built on it, and keeping anonymous email possible.

Its operational goals include being transparent to recipients that do not support it, and treating a failed verification the same as no signature, so such mail returns to normal filtering. It also aims for incremental adoption, little new infrastructure, and flexible deployment choices.

The RFC contrasts DKIM with earlier signature work (PEM, PGP and OpenPGP, MOSS and S/MIME). DKIM uses a key-centric scheme where the owner of the SDID vouches for the key, not a trusted third party, and it publishes keys in the existing DNS rather than building a new query system.
sections.eli5: DKIM stamps mail with the name of a company, not a person, and it does not get in the way of people whose mail programs do not know about it. If the seal looks broken, the mail is just treated like mail with no seal.

sections.title: How Signing and Verification Work
sections.content:
A signer chooses an SDID, hashes the selected header fields and the body, encodes that information with a private key together with other signing parameters, and adds the result in a new DKIM-Signature: header field. The signer explicitly lists which headers are signed, such as From:, Date: and Subject:. Choosing a minimal set makes the signature more robust against intermediary mail handlers.

The SDID alone is not enough to look up the key. A domain can have several keys or signers, so the signature also carries a selector. The selector is an opaque string reserved to the signer, which keeps it possible to move from an old or compromised key to a new one.

A verifier takes the domain and selector from the header field, queries the DNS for the public key, and checks the signature. Any agent on the path can verify, though it is typically done in the recipient's Administrative Management Domain. An organization can also use different subdomains as the SDID (for example newsletter.example.com versus transaction.example.com) so that assessments stay independent.
sections.eli5: The sender seals the letter with a private stamp. The receiver looks up the matching stamp pattern in a public phone book (the DNS), using a label called the selector, and checks that the seal fits.

sections.title: Service Architecture
sections.content:
DKIM relies on external services for key retrieval (DNS) and for relaying mail (SMTP). Work is split between a signing Administrative Management Domain (ADMD) and a verifying one. Signing may be done by a mail user agent, submission agent or transfer agent in the originating ADMD. Verifying may happen in a transfer agent, delivery agent or user agent in the delivering ADMD.

Three kinds of outside information need administration: the Key Store (the signer must publish a key in the DNS for every selector and SDID combination and have policies for distributing and revising keys), reputation or accreditation data about the domain, and published Signing Practices. If a signature passes, reputation information is used to assess the signer. If it fails or there is no signature from the author's domain, signing practices can be fetched to help decide whether the author's domain was used without authorization. All of this feeds a message filtering engine, whose details are out of scope.

The RFC expects DKIM most often in the outbound and inbound mail infrastructure of organizations, such as a boundary transfer agent, and less often in user agents because of higher administration and support costs. A Mediator such as a mailing list can repost a message, and a signature can survive some modifications. The Mediator can add its own signature. If a message has more than one valid signature, the order of assessment is not defined by DKIM.
sections.eli5: One mail office stamps the letter, and another mail office checks the stamp. Along the way they can look up the stamp pattern, check how well-known the sender is, and read the sender's published rules, then decide what to do with the letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This overview does not discuss threats itself. It points to the DKIM base specification, RFC 4871, for the security considerations of the protocol, with RFC 4686 as their basis.
sections.eli5: This guide does not list the dangers itself. It sends you to the other documents that do.
